title: Aggettivi e Pronomi Possessivi
subtitle: My, your, his/her — possessives that agree with the thing owned, not the owner.
objectives: Use possessive adjectives that agree with the noun possessed
Use the article with most possessives, except for singular family members
Use possessive pronouns to avoid repeating the noun

content.intro: Italian possessives are one of the biggest grammatical differences from English: they agree with the thing owned, not with the owner — so suo can mean "his" or "her", depending only on what's possessed and by whom in context.
content.explanation: Possessives are almost always preceded by the definite article, agreeing with both the article and the noun: il mio libro, la mia casa, i miei libri, le mie case. The one major exception is singular, unmodified family members, which drop the article: mio padre, tua sorella — but the article returns with a plural family noun or a modified one: i miei genitori, la mia sorella maggiore.

rules.heading: a) Agreement
rules.body: Mio/tuo/suo/nostro/vostro each have four forms (-o/-a/-i/-e) agreeing with the noun possessed. Loro never changes: il loro libro, la loro casa, i loro libri.

rules.heading: b) Singular family members drop the article
rules.body:
• mio fratello, tua madre, suo zio (no article)
  • but: i miei fratelli (plural — article returns)
  • and: la mia sorella maggiore (modified by an adjective — article returns)

rules.heading: c) Possessive pronouns
rules.body: Same forms, used alone to avoid repeating the noun: Questo è il mio libro. Dov'è il tuo? (This is my book. Where's yours?)

examples.it: Il tuo è più grande del mio.

commonMistakes.why: Singular, unmodified family members drop the article — the article only returns for plurals or modified nouns.
The possessive and article must agree with libro (masculine), not with the owner's gender.

commonMistakes.right: il loro figlio / i loro figli
commonMistakes.why: The article must match the number of the noun; loro itself never changes but the article and noun must agree with each other.

items.prompt: ___ (my) sorella lavora in banca. (family, singular, unmodified)
items.explanation: Singular, unmodified family member drops the article: mia sorella.
Casa is not a family member, so it keeps its article: la nostra.
Loro is invariable but the article agrees with amici (masc. plural): i loro.
Suo agrees with macchina, a feminine noun: la sua macchina.

summary: Possessive adjectives agree with the thing possessed, not the owner — suo can mean his or her.
Almost always used with the article, except before a singular, unmodified family member.
Loro never changes form, but the article before it still agrees with the noun.
